summary: Tolbutamide is a short-acting first-generation sulfonylurea used with diet to lower blood glucose in type 2 (non-insulin-dependent) diabetes. It stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels. It carries a BOXED WARNING regarding increased cardiovascular mortality, based on the University Group Diabetes Program (UGDP) study, which found a higher rate of cardiovascular death with tolbutamide than with diet alone or diet plus insulin. The principal adverse effect is hypoglycaemia (more likely with missed meals, renal/hepatic impairment, the elderly, and alcohol). It has been largely superseded by newer agents.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

dosage.d: About 1-2 g daily by mouth (some start lower at 0.25-0.5 g), as a single morning dose or in divided doses
0.25-2 g daily; usual maintenance around 0.25-1.5 g/day; maximum ~3 g/day
dosage.n: Doses above ~2 g rarely add benefit

dosage.d: Lower starting and maintenance doses; titrate cautiously

admin: Take with meals to reduce stomach upset and align the glucose-lowering effect with food intake
Do not skip meals while taking it - this risks hypoglycaemia
Larger total daily doses are often divided (e.g. morning and evening)
Combine with diet, weight control and exercise

moa: Tolbutamide binds the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1) on pancreatic beta cells, closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels. The resulting membrane depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the rise in intracellular calcium triggers insulin secretion. Its glucose-lowering effect therefore depends on functioning beta cells; it does not lower glucose in their absence.

absolute: Severe hepatic or renal impairment with marked hypoglycaemia risk
relative: Significant cardiovascular disease (boxed CV mortality concern)
Conditions causing irregular eating or alcohol use
monitor: Fasting and self-monitored blood glucose; HbA1c
Full blood count if cytopenia suspected

preg: Not recommended in pregnancy; insulin is preferred for glycaemic control. Sulfonylureas cross the placenta and prolonged neonatal hypoglycaemia has been reported, particularly if given near delivery.
lact: Generally avoided during breastfeeding; sulfonylureas may pass into milk and could cause hypoglycaemia in the infant - monitor the infant's glucose if used.
renal: Use with caution and at reduced doses in renal impairment; reduced clearance of the drug/metabolites increases the risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia. Avoid in severe impairment.
hepatic: Tolbutamide is hepatically metabolised; use cautiously at reduced doses in hepatic impairment because impaired metabolism increases hypoglycaemia risk. Avoid in severe liver disease.

major: Other glucose-lowering agents (insulin, sulfonylureas) - additive hypoglycaemia
Drugs that potentiate hypoglycaemia: sulfonamides, azole antifungals (CYP2C9 inhibitors), fluconazole, NSAIDs, salicylates, warfarin - increase tolbutamide effect/levels
moderate: Beta-blockers - may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms and impair recovery
Drugs that raise glucose/reduce effect: thiazides, corticosteroids, rifampin, phenytoin, sympathomimetics, oral contraceptives
minor: Highly protein-bound drugs may transiently displace tolbutamide
interactions.food: Take with food to lessen GI upset; align dosing with meals to avoid hypoglycaemia.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - it increases the risk of hypoglycaemia and can produce a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea) with sulfonylureas.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers blood glucose (the therapeutic marker); can rarely affect blood counts, liver enzymes and thyroid-related tests.

serious: Severe skin reactions / disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
emergency: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizures or loss of consciousness

monitoring: Clinical signs of hypoglycaemia, especially with missed meals or alcohol
Full blood count if cytopenia is suspected
counsel: Take with meals and never skip meals, or your blood sugar can drop too low
Learn the signs of low blood sugar (shaking, sweating, hunger, confusion) and how to treat them with fast sugar
Avoid alcohol - it can cause low blood sugar and a flushing reaction
Keep up your diet, exercise and regular blood-sugar checks
Report yellowing of the skin/eyes, unusual bleeding, fever/sore throat, or frequent low blood sugars
pk: Peak plasma concentration around 3-4 hours; maximal hypoglycaemic effect ~5-8 hours
Store tablets at room temperature, protected from moisture and light
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased cardiovascular mortality (UGDP study) - a class concern for sulfonylureas highlighted with tolbutamide
Short-acting first-generation sulfonylurea, largely superseded by second-generation agents and newer classes
Hypoglycaemia is the main danger - higher with missed meals, alcohol, renal/hepatic impairment and in the elderly
CYP2C9 inhibitors (e.g. fluconazole, sulfonamides) and protein-binding displacers potentiate hypoglycaemia
Use insulin rather than sulfonylureas in pregnancy
missed: If a dose is missed, take it with the next meal if it is soon; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the usual schedule. Do not double the dose, and do not take it without eating, to avoid hypoglycaemia.
overdose: Overdose causes hypoglycaemia, which may be severe and prolonged. Treat conscious patients with oral carbohydrate; give IV dextrose (and admit/observe for many hours because of the risk of recurrence) for severe or symptomatic hypoglycaemia. Octreotide can be used for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia. Monitor glucose closely and provide supportive care.
